title: Event Triggered Execution: PowerShell Profile
summary: PowerShell reads profile scripts at the start of every session, unless the interpreter is launched with the NoProfile switch. There is a profile for all users and all hosts, one for all users of a single host program, one for the current user across hosts, and one for the current user in a specific host such as the console, the integrated scripting environment or an editor. Each is a file named profile.ps1 in a documented location. An adversary appends commands to a profile so that the code runs whenever a shell opens, which gives persistence in the user's context and, if an administrator opens PowerShell, execution with that administrator's rights. The artefacts are file writes to the profile paths, script block logging records, module logging records, transcription files where enabled, and process creation for the PowerShell host without the NoProfile switch. Legitimate profile content is common on administration workstations, so the discriminator is a change in content, an obfuscated or download-based command, or a profile on a host where nobody customises shells.

beginner.definition: This technique hides commands in a PowerShell profile. A profile is a script that PowerShell runs each time it starts. It exists so people can set up their own shortcuts and settings. An attacker adds their own commands to that script. The commands then run every time the user opens PowerShell. This sub-technique differs from its parent because opening a shell, and not a sign in, sets off the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: The profile runs quietly with every new shell, so the attacker's commands look like part of normal administration. If an administrator opens PowerShell on the same machine, the profile may run with much higher rights than the author had. Logs often record the commands, but only if the logging features were switched on first. If you ignore this file, a small edit can keep an intruder active for a long time.
howItWorks: PowerShell reads a set of profile scripts every time a new session starts.
There are profiles for all users, for a single user, and for each host program such as the console.
Each profile is a file named profile.ps1, and it lives in a documented folder.
An attacker adds commands to that file, so the code runs with each new session.
The NoProfile switch stops profile loading, but it only affects the session that uses the switch.
If an administrator opens PowerShell, the same profile may run with higher rights than the author had.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with a note beside the kettle. Everyone reads the note before making tea. If someone adds a line that says also unlock the back door, every flatmate follows it without noticing. The PowerShell profile is that note. PowerShell reads it at the start of every session, and most users never look at what it says.
takeaways: A PowerShell profile is read at every session start unless the NoProfile switch is used.
Profile content runs in the context of whoever opens the shell.
Turn on script block logging and check profile files for unexpected changes.

objectives: Explain what a PowerShell profile is and when it runs.
List the profile scopes and the host programs that use them.
Describe how a profile gives both persistence and higher rights.
Identify the PowerShell logging features that record profile commands.
Recognise an unexpected change in a profile file.
Explain the effect and the limits of the NoProfile switch.
